title: Skyroot Aerospace Set to Make History With Vikram-1 Launch on July 18, India's First Private Orbital Rocket

body:
Key Takeaways
  • Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 is India's first private orbital rocket, launching on July 18.
  • The company raised $60 million, doubling its valuation to $1.1 billion.
  • Vikram-1 can carry payloads up to 350 kg into low Earth orbit.
  • The launch signifies a shift in India's private space sector alongside ISRO.
  • Skyroot's journey showcases India's growing deep-tech innovation on the global stage.

India's first private orbital rocket, Vikram-1, is set to launch from Sriharikota on July 18, marking a watershed moment for the country's space industry. Hyderabad-based Skyroot Aerospace, which became India's first spacetech unicorn after raising $60 million at a $1.1 billion valuation, is preparing for the historic mission.

From ISRO Engineers to Unicorn Founders

Founded in 2018 by former ISRO scientists Pawan Kumar Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka, Skyroot has moved from concept to orbital launch in under eight years. The company describes Vikram-1 as a "cab to space" — a vehicle that satellite companies and institutions can use to place payloads of up to 350 kg into low Earth orbit.

"This mission is designed as both a technology demonstration and a learning mission," said Naga Bharath Daka, Skyroot's COO and co-founder.

The rocket features 3D-printed engines and a carbon-fibre composite structure, designed for rapid manufacturing. Skyroot's new Infinity campus in Hyderabad has the capacity to build one rocket per month.

Global Investors Signal Confidence

Skyroot's $60 million funding round was co-led by Sherpalo Ventures and Singapore sovereign wealth fund GIC, with structured debt from BlackRock. The investment more than doubled the company's valuation from $500 million in 2023.

Ram Shriram, founder of Sherpalo Ventures and known for his early backing of Google, has joined Skyroot's board. His involvement, along with backing from GIC and BlackRock, sends what industry observers call a "strong signal" about India's private space sector.

"The presence of GIC, BlackRock and Ram Sriram on the cap table implies a thesis that India's launch market is a multi-decade infrastructure story, not a speculative tech bet," said Vipul Patel of IIMA Ventures.

What Vikram-1 Means for India's Space Ambitions

The launch comes at a significant moment — following consecutive orbital launch failures by ISRO — and represents India's private sector stepping up alongside the national agency. Skyroot was the first startup to sign an agreement to use ISRO's launch and test facilities when the government opened the sector to private companies in 2020.

Lt. Gen. A.K. Bhatt (Retd.), Director General of the Indian Space Association, called the development "a landmark for India's private space ecosystem," noting it could strengthen India's ambitions of increasing its share of the global space economy by 2033.

The maiden Vikram-1 launch is also opening doors for public engagement — viewing gallery registrations at Sriharikota are now open for the July 18 launch.

For the Indian diaspora, Skyroot's journey resonates deeply — former ISRO engineers building a globally competitive launch company, backed by Silicon Valley investors, represents the kind of deep-tech innovation that India is increasingly known for on the world stage.
